en: *Rāmarudrī*:
"Necessarily present" means [the property of] not occurring in that which possesses occasional substancehood (*naimitika-dravyatva*).

The sense is that, since fluidity (*dravatva*) must necessarily be included to exclude earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like, and because it is necessarily present, it would be improper to omit it and instead introduce color (*rūpa*), which is not so present. As for the phrase "composed of color" (*rūpaghaṭita*), the sense is that in this context the word *varṇa* has the meaning of "color."

Even if this were so, since the term "white" (*śukla*) is also mentioned in the original [definition], and since that term does not fit the stated definition, the contradiction with the original text remains unavoidable; nevertheless, in this context,
one must introduce either "subsisting in what is white" (*śuklavadvṛttitva*) or "subsisting in what possesses color" (*rūpavadvṛttitva*).

The point is that there is no contradiction with the root text (*mūla*), because the intention of the root is intended to be expressed in both definitions due to the absence of a decisive criterion for choosing between them. Regarding the phrase "in this very way" and so forth: since the two words *śukla* (white) and *rūpa* (form) are not included in one definition, it should be understood that the other definition in the root text follows the *kārikā*.

Regarding the term "bodhya" (to be understood): the inclusion of both "subsisting in that which possesses color" (*rūpavadvṛttitva*) and "being directly pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpyatva*) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when taking airness (*vāyutva*) as the subject, and for the purpose of excluding it when taking clothness (*paṭatva*) and so forth. This is the meaning according to Rāmarudrī.

Nor [is there a problem], because since qualities such as blue are also established by experience in cloth, [the definition] is indeed [excluded] by the phrase "not co-locating" (*asamānādhikaraṇānta*).

It should not be argued that since the exclusion of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) and so forth is possible, the direct purpose of the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is merely to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conch shells and the like, and thus the mention of "it is exactly thus" is irrelevant;
for in cases such as a blue cloth, the color blue does not belong to the cloth itself, but rather to a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) endowed with blue.

From the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is simply neuter. The meaning is that although there is a lexicon stating "words such as *śukla* [denoting quality] are masculine," just as usages such as *śuklaṃ rūpam* (white color) are observed in works like the *Cintāmaṇi*, so too is it here. As for the lexicon...
The sense is that its application occurs only in cases where there is no co-occurrence with a word denoting the substantive (viśeṣya).

It should be understood that in the root-text beginning with "dravyatva" (substantiality), no definition was provided for the nature of water as possessing cold touch, because there is no defect whatsoever in taking that as the definition of water. Regarding the phrase "the rest":
The phrase "subsisting in that which possesses sweetness" (*madhuravadvṛtti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking *vāyutva* (the nature of air) as the [defining property].

The phrase "directly pervaded" (*sākṣādvyāpya*) is included to exclude over-extension by taking *śarkarātva* (the nature of sugar) as the [defining property]. The word "universal" (*jāti*) is included to exclude over-extension by taking the common property of being both water and sugar; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the term *upaṣṭambhaka*: it means "conjoined with the waters of the Yamunā. However, this must be understood: the author of the root text intends that the apprehension of blueness in the Yamunā's water is due to its being conditioned by its substrate—that is, it is produced solely by a defect consisting in conjunction with a particular substrate.

However, it cannot be that [the cognition] consists in the relation of the aforementioned series; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving earthiness in water, just as one perceives blueness. Nor can it be argued that, even in your own view, the cognition of earthiness does not arise due to the force of such a defect.

It is established by the universal experience of all that, in the case of a transparent substance such as crystal, it is only the non-perception of redness— and not the perception of cloth-ness— that occurs due to the influence of contact with a red cloth; therefore,
just as one postulates that a defect such as jaundice (pittadoṣa) produces only the illusion of yellowness, so too here [one must accept this] in accordance with experience.
Since only the capacity to produce the illusion of blueness needs to be postulated in such a defect,

it is precisely because the illusion is produced by that specific defect that even those who possess discerning vision experience the illusion of blueness through inherence (samavāya) alone; for [otherwise] there would be no difference between "the pot is blue" and "the water is blue."

Someone might maintain that the distinctness [of the taste] from water is established by experience. Anticipating the deficiency in the root text— since it states, for example, "of the consumption of *harītakī*," that the consumption of *harītakī* manifests the taste of water without providing a reason for this— the author provides the reason.
He completes [the argument] with the words "because of its being a manifestor" (*vyañjakatvāt*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the *harītakī*":

although, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the postulation of a sweet taste in the *harītakī* is equivalent to the postulation of a sweet taste in water, and thus its demonstration would be inappropriate due to the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*), nevertheless, [it is mentioned] because the opponent [thinks] in my view...

If it is argued that, in your view, the addition of a single causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is equivalent to the postulation of a sweet taste in water, then our postulation of that [causal relation] in water is equivalent to your postulation of a sweet taste in the *harītakī* fruit.
It should be understood that this mention [of the property] is intended to indicate that, according to your own view, it is indeed excessive.

Since the earthness (*pṛthivītva*) that delimits the capacity to produce sourness is absent in water, the statement in the root-text—that water does not possess sourness and the like—is inconsistent. This is because [earthness] also serves as the delimitant of the capacity to produce sweetness in substances such as sugar.

He raises the objection—beginning with "Even though"—on the grounds that since *pṛthivītva* (earthness) has already been established [as the determinant], its absence in water would entail the non-existence of sweet taste and so forth. In this context, "in the *harītakī*" refers to the fact that [the sweetness] is necessary, which means it is based on empirical experience (*anubhava*). As for the phrase "by way of *jalatva* (waterhood)"...

"By means of earthness alone," and so forth. Now, one might raise the objection that it is difficult to find a decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*) as to whether the taste residing in the citron appears in the water, or the taste residing in the water appears in the citron; in response to this doubt, he says: "Even when [the citron] is dried. And it is not thus...
Since it is sufficient to accept that the sweet taste residing in the *harītakī* appears in the water through a causal series, one might argue that there would be no sweet taste in the water at all;
therefore, he says: "In the *harītakī*" and "and its manifester."
The meaning is that *harītakī* (myrobalan) is the manifestor of the sweet taste (*madhurarasavyañjaka*). "Of another taste" refers to the astringent taste (*kaṣāyarasa*).

"By the force of the fruit" means by the force of the effect in the form of its direct perception (*tatpratyakṣarūpakāryabala*). "Due to the absence of proof" means that if a variegated taste (*citrarasa*) were unestablished by valid cognition, it could not be accepted—just as a variegated color (*citrarūpa*) [is not accepted]—on the grounds that it resides in the parts.

The collective meaning is that because there is no production of any single taste due to mutual opposition among the various flavorful components within a substance, and because of the absence of such destruction [of the opposing qualities], the myrobalan (*harītakī*) is indeed "tasteless. Nor is it the case that, upon eating the myrobalan, the perception of that [taste] would not occur, for it is indeed experienced.

Therefore, he says "But the cognition of taste... regarding the perception of the astringent taste. [The phrase] "by way of succession" (paramparayā) means through the relation of being inherent in that which is inherent in its own substratum. [The term] "is rejected" implies that the sweetness in the water of the Gaṅgā is established by direct perception. Now, one might object: even in ghee and the like, it is only the water contained therein [that possesses sweetness].

Regarding the term "viscosity" (*sneha*): it is incorrect [to claim] that it is the root [cause] of ghee and the like, because since these are composed of earth (*pārthiva*), aqueous viscosity cannot exist therein. Therefore, he completes the argument with the words "of water alone," etc.
"Only the state of being produced water" (*janyajalatvam eva*) means: only the universal (*jāti*) residing in all produced water.

He says "tadavacchinna" (delimited by that) for the purpose of establishing the nature of water (*jalatva*) in an atom; the meaning is "delimited by produced-water-ness" (*janyajalatva*). Regarding "samaniyata" (co-extensive): the point is that this very [lack of distinction] is the obstacle to the apprehension of the difference between two universals (*jāti*). "Apre'pi" (also later on): [this applies] even to the apprehension of the difference between the two universals residing in fire (*tejas*).

The sense is that this alone is the obstacle. ||39|| Regarding "from that which is in the genitive case" (*ṣaṣṭhīsamarthāt*): the meaning is that the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the genitive, with the intention that it is like [the suffix applied] after a word in the nominative. Also later on, in the definition of light (*tejaḥ*), the phrase "in water alone" (*jalamātre*) means in pure water. "But that" (*sa tu*): the meaning is "but such a reading. Straightforward (*ṛjuḥ*).

The meaning is clear. This has been stated: "occasional liquidity" (naimitikadravatva) has been mentioned; the sense is that this is because heat alone is established as the efficient cause (nimitta). And that occasional liquidity—[it is mentioned] because only that [liquidity] which is innate (sāṃsiddhika) serves as the manifestor of the nature of water (jalatva). This is the sense. (Rāmarudrī)

The phrase "because of its destruction" refers to [the destruction] of the hailstone, and so forth. In the root text, the phrase "by a particular unseen force" (adṛṣṭaviśeṣeṇa) means "by the power of bad karma" (duradṛṣṭabala). Obstruction is non-perception; thus, when fluidity is not perceived due to the force of an obstructing factor, the cognition of hardness is merely an error.

This is the state [of the object]. (40) Thus ends the "Jalagrantha" (The Knot on Water). Regarding the term "vivakṣaṇa" (desire to speak): according to Rāmarudrī, it means "produced by a blue part. The mention of "blue" is illustrative, as red and other colors may also arise through the process of baking (pāka).

He establishes the absence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by stating "luminosity" (*bhāsvaratvam*). Now, one might raise the objection that since the colors belonging to fire (*tejas*) are of many kinds, luminosity cannot constitute a universal (*jāti*) due to its commingling (*sāṃkarya*) with yellowness, whiteness, and so forth. To this [he replies]:

He refutes [the objection] with the words "and [it is] pervaded by whiteness. One might object: "Since even in lightning and similar phenomena, a bright yellow is experienced, how can it be said that its [color] is white? The point is that we simply accept that there is an error regarding yellowness in respect to that very whiteness present there. [Regarding the phrase] "not having color as its object": and it is not...

It must be asked: since there is no experience of the color-form (*rūpa*) being the object even in the initial non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) such as "this is a jar," how can this [claim] be maintained? For at the time of the sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with the jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), there is necessarily also sensory contact with the color-form and so forth.

The point is that, just as in the case of a pot and pot-ness, so too in the case of color and color-ness, even the initial non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) which apprehends a collection (*samūhālambana*)—

namely, the first determinate perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*)— must be accepted as having color as its object precisely because it does not apprehend the qualifiedness of color-ness (*rūpatvaviśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*). This is what is indicated by the word "sūcita" (indicated).

The phrase "of Vaiśvānara and so forth" implies that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is to be understood as a remainder (*śeṣa*). Regarding the term "earthy" (*pārthiva*): it means "by way of an earthy color produced by heating" (*pākaja*).

Since that [color] alone is produced by heating, the kind of color perceived in Vaiśvānara is not the same kind of color previously experienced in earth such as wood; therefore, its being produced by heating (*pākajatva*) has been demonstrated.

The object of meditation. Now, one might object: "In the root text, the presence of occasional fluidity (*naimitikadravatva*) in the brilliance of gold-form was demonstrated, but that is indeed useless, since even by that much the [definition's] lack of over-extension (*avyāpti*) remains unrefuted. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By that... (*tena*).
The meaning is: "by means of stating that. And thus, the purpose of that text is precisely to avoid the impossibility [of the definition].

The intention is that the avoidance of under-extension (*avyāpti*), however, must be accomplished by the subsequent text itself. Regarding the phrase "not subsisting in earth" (*pṛthivyavṛtti*): here, although the word "genus" (*jāti*) refers to a genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*).

It is stated that "being directly pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpya*) is merely for the purpose of indicating that there is no [other] way out (*nistāra*). (Rāmarudrī) One should observe that "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator), because otherwise there would be the possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) even to air and so forth, by taking "air-ness" (*vāyutva*) and the like as the basis. 41. Regarding the term "touch" (*sparśapada*).

The phrase "belonging to another" (*parakīya*) is included to prevent the failure of the example in the case of a lamp, which manifests its own touch. The qualification "provided it exists" (*sati*) in the reason is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of water, which—according to the aforementioned method—manifests the color of another. The qualifying portion of the predicate (*viśeṣyadala*) is for the purpose of excluding [the property] from space (*gagana*) and so forth. [Finally, this applies] to a jar and other such things which manifest their own color.

To exclude that [case], the term "belonging to another" (*parakīya*) must also be applied there. Furthermore, to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the contact of the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃnikarṣa*), the phrase "provided it is a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) should also be supplied. It should be understood that all of this has been omitted because it was already stated in the root text. The audacious view that the eyeball itself is the eye and is not composed of light (*taijasa*)—

He demonstrates this with the words "In this regard, some... and so forth. "Unconnected with the object" means lacking contact with the object. By the word "only" (*eva*), the capacity to grasp what is in close proximity is excluded, because the eye does not perceive that which is merely conjoined with the eyeball (*golaka*).
Here, the term "eye" refers to that which is intended as the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*); by that [term],...
It should be understood that even though, in our own view, the eye consisting of light-form (*tejorūpa*) does not exist, there is no lack of establishment of the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*);

nor is there a failure of the subsequent argument beginning with "if" (*yadi*), because the terrestrial globe (*pārthivagolaka*) is not admitted by him [the opponent] to be the perceiver of what is near. And here, regarding the capacity to indicate...

It should be understood that by accepting that [position], the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "yadi" (if) would not arise. And here, in accordance with the subsequent text, the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "because it would be a grasper of what is unconnected to its substratum"—is to be inferred; however, [the opponent might argue] that in the act of perception there must be both direct confrontation (*ābhimukhya*) and lack of intervention (*avyavadhāna*).

In this view, it must necessarily be accepted as the *prayojaka* (the causal factor); otherwise, it would be impossible to prevent the visual perception of objects situated behind [an obstacle] or those that are obstructed. However, according to the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), [this is avoided] precisely by the absence of contact with the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga-abhāva*).
Since that [objection] can be refuted, it need not be postulated for them; however, it should be understood that the postulation of remoteness as an impediment is common to both systems.
Now, to dispel the doubt that the stated reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), [the author states] that the reason itself [is absent] in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve*).

He demonstrates a favorable *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) in the form of the consequence that [the opponent's view] would not be possible, thereby resulting in the destruction of the cause (*hetūcchitti*), beginning with the words "If... and so forth. The term "prāpyaprakāśakāri" means that which grasps what is in close proximity.
The word "nacaivam" is to be read as a separate phrase; its meaning is: "and it does not grasp merely that which is connected to the physical eye-organ (*golaka*)."

The passage beginning with "by the eye" (*cakṣuṣā*) and ending with "because of apprehension" (*grahaṇāt*) [is intended here]. Here, having considered the lack of conviction regarding the form of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that will be stated in the case of the light of a lamp (*pradīpaprabhā*), the probandum as stated is established for the eye even by its being the grasper of a substance possessing a dimension greater than its own.

He says "moreover" (*kiṃca*) to show that [the objection] is possible. With the intention of stating a general pervasion (*sāmānyamukhavyāpti*)—namely, that whatever is conjoined with something and produces a result related to it cannot have a dimension absolutely smaller than that thing—he provides an example, saying "indeed not" (*na khalu*). [The example is] a nail-painter (*nakharañjanikā*).

[Otherwise,] it would be like a nail-cutter; likewise, if one does not accept this pervasion, even a nail-painter would cut down a great log that is split by an axe. And here, since we observe that even a log larger than itself can be split by an axe, [there is no proof of] absolute minuteness.
Because it is impossible to provide a [satisfactory] definition, he states another reason out of this dissatisfaction: "The branch...

The sense is that, since the branch and the moon are both causes of a visual perception occurring at the same time, it would be possible to establish that the eye perceives what is not in contact [with it].

He provides the summary: "And thus" (*evaṃca*). This means: "and [the view] that the eye perceives what is not in contact [with it]. Anticipating the objection that this might be an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "And that. Thus, since it would result in a contradiction with the verse stating "the sense organ is the eye," an accepted consequence is not possible.
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "unconnected with its substratum":

the point is that the aforementioned rule is contradicted in the case of the light of a lamp, which perceives objects such as a jar that are not connected to the lamp’s own substratum (the wick). "That misconception" refers to the illusion of simultaneity. [This occurs] due to the proximity in time.
Because it occurs at an extremely proximate time. [Objection: But surely, since the moon is very far from the branch, there can be no immediate contact between the eye and the moon.

He says, "For [the proximity] is inconceivable," meaning that it is impossible for there to be an absolute proximity between the branch and the moon when both are being perceived by the eye, such that an illusion of simultaneity could arise; the meaning is that this is due to an extreme lightness, which implies an excellence of motion that generates velocity.

It should be understood that lightness, which consists in the absence of heaviness, cannot possibly possess an excellence in comparison to air and other such substances. "Yat" means "because. "Prācīnācala" is the mountain of sunrise;
"cūḍā" means the top or the summit. "Mayūkhamālini" refers to the Sun; "abhimāna" is a delusion.
The point is that the "climbing of the mountain of sunrise" and the "spreading of rays" cannot be simultaneous according to the actual nature of things.
However, in reality, since the inference establishing the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of the visual organ (*cakṣurindriya*) has already been stated previously...

Since the inference proving that the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is composed of light (*taijasa*) has already been stated previously, the status of the eyeball (*golaka*) as the eye-faculty is not even a subject for doubt; for the proponents of our own school do not [accept it] merely out of deference to the theory of reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*).

The suchness (tathātva) of the eye is thus accepted; otherwise, how could the distinctness of the tongue-faculty and others from their physical bases be established? Although there is no evidence whatsoever for the nose-faculty being distinct from its base because it is composed of earth (pārthiva), nevertheless—

It should be understood that its existence is established because, even when the nose is present, some people are observed not to perceive odors, and because of the inference: "The olfactory and other sense organs are supersensible (atīndriya), because they are sense organs, like the mind. External light is not [required] here.

It should be understood that [the light in question] is indeed fire possessing non-manifest color (*anudbhūtarūpa*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of atoms of sunlight and so forth, as well as the objects composed of them, becoming perceptible. The phrase "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) implies that the property of being "belonging to another" (*parakīyatva*) is not included [in the definition]. "Possessing yellow color" (*pītarūpavat*) refers to [the example of] a pot and the like.

The meaning is: "of the supporting portion consisting of earth. (Rāmarudrī) Regarding the phrase "in the Dharmaśāstra": the meaning is that it takes the form of "one should give gold weighing one *tolaka*," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of remaining in that state": since the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), [the proof] occurs through co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The sense is that it would lead to the consequence of sublation (*bādhaprasaṅga*). Even if the probandum (*sādhya*) were established through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), since gold can possibly be an object of the nature of fire (*taijasa*), sublation through co-referentiality would not constitute a defect in the establishment of the probandum; thus, [there remains] the state of being denotable by the word "gold."

Even if it were the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), there would be no deficiency. For, according to the etymological derivation "that which possesses a beautiful color" (*śobhano varṇo yasya*), even lamps and the like are understood by the word *suvarṇa*; thus, one must reflect that the proof of gold being an object of light is not established [by this]. [This is stated] in terms of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Regarding the phrase "of the proven-proven" (*siddhasādhanasya*): even if it is granted that, in the locus of the employed reason, an inference must be admitted as arising solely from the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)— since there is no prior ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through any other inference— even so, in the case of negative concomitance, there is a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum and the probans.

By using the term "ghaṭaka" (constituent), there is no occasion for the suspicion of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); nevertheless, since after an inference based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding silver and the like,

it is also possible to have a cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) through positive co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), an inference may subsequently arise in the case of gold with respect to that very same form by means of that cognition of positive concomitance as well.

It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that [the effect] arises. Regarding the phrase "not destroyed by contact with fire" (*agnisaṃyogānāśya*), the full expression is "by the absence of the presence of fire" (*agnisamavadhānābhāvena*), and so forth.

Consequently, since the generality of the fluidity of clarified butter (*ghṛtadravatvasāmānya*) itself is encompassed by the delimitor of the state of being destructible by contact with fire, [it follows that it is not eternal].

Even though such ghee is not well-known [in common experience], there is no deficiency, because ghee—which possesses fluidity that is not the counter-positive of a destruction produced by contact with fire due to the absence of contact with fire—is well-known. Regarding the phrase "co-inherent in the same locus" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*): [it refers to] being distinct from quality and action.

The point is that the locative absolute construction (*satisaptamī*) has already been established as having the sense of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cases such as "when the sun exists" (*satyāditye*),
and as having the sense of simultaneity (*samānakālīnatva*) in cases such as "he went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*).

Since there would otherwise be the consequence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with ether and so forth— by way of a series of conjunctions with their own inherent substrates (*svasamavāyi*) even in the case of that which possesses non-interrupted fluidity—
it is necessary to complete the sense of "substratum" (*adhikaraṇatva*) in order to establish that [fluidity] as the cause by means of inherence (*samavāya*).

He explains [the passage] beginning with "not being cut off" (*anucchidyamāna*), etc. Since it is possible for the word *drava* (liquid) to refer to a quality (*guṇa*), that which has its liquid state being cut off is "one whose liquid state is being cut off" (*ucchidyamānadrava*);

one whose liquid state is not being cut off is "one whose liquid state is not being cut off" (*anucchidyamānadrava*); the abstract state of being such is "the condition of having an uncut-off liquid state" (*tattva*).
He refutes the view that the word [‘taijasa’] possesses a meaning obtainable through etymological derivation by stating "but not" (na tu).
The phrase "because it is not a substratum" is to be construed with what precedes it.
This is because it serves as a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*): if gold were not composed of light (*taijasa*), [it would follow that...]

It might be argued that this [definition] would not hold, just as the status of being a son of Agni is established by scripture (*āgama*) alone; however, this is not the case because there exists the supporting reasoning (*tarka*).

The meaning of the word "offspring" (*apatya*) is that which has for its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) the inherent cause of its own inherent cause; it does not mean "anything produced," for if it did, undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*) would follow, such as time (*kāla*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, also being offspring.

The meaning is as follows: "A specific type of genus" (*jāti-viśeṣam*). The core point is that otherwise, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the cumbersome property of "being produced by the destruction of parts" within the definition of the delimiting factor for being produced (*janya-tāvacchedaka-koṭi*).
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "this too is refuted," it is indicated that such scripture (*āgama*) is also refuted by way of verbal testimony (*śabda-vidhayā*).
The evidence for the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of gold has been indicated. Regarding the word "kṣoda" (powder):
although [it refers to] the earthly portion (*pārthivabhāga*), [as noted by] Rāmarudrī... [ie3]... [the text continues].

At that time, even if fluidity is admitted [in fire], it can be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because another fluid substance in the form of light exists as an obstructer; nevertheless,
since water alone is established as the obstructer of the destruction of the fluidity of earthy substances, [the objection remains].

Since fire possessing occasional liquidity was unestablished prior to its inference, it is not possible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by taking the existence of its obstructors as the cause;
rather, the postulation of a distinct substance is based on its being the obstructor of the destruction of the liquidity of earthy substances.
The sense is that [the author] follows precisely the alternative view (matāntara) which will be stated starting with the words "having gone" (*paretu*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of golden [objects] consisting of light" (*taijasa-suvarṇe’pi*): because the reason (*hetu*) consisting of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*)—which is yet to be stated there—is absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a partial unestablished reason (*bhāgāsiddhi*), since the intended object of proof is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*).
This is the state of affairs. Therefore, in the case of a dry, yellow earthen substance devoid of contact with fire,
there is the probandum— the conjunction with a liquid substance of a different class— and the reason—
the property of not being the locus of a color different from its own preceding color at the time of the fire-contact that is co-located with itself.

The term "in contact with fire" (agnisaṃyogī) is purposeful for the purpose of excluding both the sublation (bādhā) and the unestablished nature (asiddhi) due to non-existence. Furthermore, in this context, since the probandum (sādhya) is established for both disputants in some yellow cloth and so forth, if the probandum were intended as being co-located (sāmānādhikaraṇyena), it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana); therefore, [the probandum must be established] only by way of the delimiting factor (avacchedakāvacchedena).

It should be understood that the intended purpose is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Therefore, [the argument applies] to a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu*). Although the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the previous reason remains exactly the same even in the case of a water-atom—since "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) would still be a qualification of the reason, resulting in the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvaprasiddhi*) there as well—[the following applies].

It should be understood that although there is an absence of destructible fluidity (*nāśyadravatva*) in earth due to its contact with fire, there is no deviation [in the definition] because it is accepted that the term "fluidity" (*dravatva*) in that context refers to adventitious fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*).

Regarding the word "contrary" (*virodhī*): it means "that which obstructs a heterogeneous color" (*vijātīyarūpapratibandhaka*). [This applies to] that which is other than a fluid substance (*dravadravya*). — Rāmarudrī.

The meaning is "unseen force" (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of its impossibility there": the sense is that natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) is not experienced there [in air]. Regarding the phrase "in air and so forth":
although even light does not have its color perceived there, the absence of color is not the basis for postulating an obstructive quality in air.

Nevertheless, if the conjunction with the substance water were the inhibitor of the destruction of earth-color, then the destruction of earth-color through baking would never occur anywhere, because that [conjunction] would always be present; therefore,
it must be some other substance possessing color.
It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that suchness must be accepted.

"At that time" means during the state of remaining in darkness. "Caused by the perception of its own kind" refers to that yellow color which is of the same class as itself by virtue of being color (*rūpatva*).

The meaning is that non-apprehension caused by that [absence] is the absence of being an object of perception. Regarding the phrase "distinct from light": since one does not admit a conjunction of a thing with itself as its own counter-correlative, the perception of light would otherwise be impossible if it were not conjoined with another light; therefore, it must be so.

The sense is that the relation of cause and effect must be accepted. Although this inconsistency would not arise if conjunction inherent in light were taken as the cause— since that [conjunction] exists in light as well— nevertheless, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is light itself [that is the cause], by way of the relation of conjunction.

The sense is that, since it must be accepted that [the eye] is a cause for the direct perception of a substance, and because a thing cannot be conjoined with itself, the qualification "distinct from light" (*tejobhinna*) is necessary as a modifier of the substance. Regarding the word "quickly" (*drutam*): this refers to the yellow substance [of the conch], according to the maxim of the ink-powder situated in water.
This was stated with the author’s intention, since he accepts the admission of fluidity (*adravatva*).

The particle *api* in the phrase "of fluidity also" (*dravatvasyāpi*) is to be construed immediately after "due to its cessation" (*ucchedāt*); thus, even though fluidity exists in water, [the argument applies] to that specific fluidity of it.
The meaning is that it is not water because it is extremely distinct from the liquidity of earth and because its liquidity is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*).
— Rāmarudrī.
And because it possesses a yellow color, he states that earth is not something other [than that], saying: "of earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvasya*). Now, one might ask:

why is there no destruction of color when there is contact with fire? To this he says: "the destruction of color," and so forth. The use of the word "they say" (*vadanti*) is intended to indicate a lack of conviction [on the part of the author]. And that [lack of conviction] arises because it is possible to admit, even in the case of the earthly [substance], the presence of fluidity at that time.

Because validity is possible through cognition, and because the conjunction with another substance is already established elsewhere as the preventer of the destruction of color and fluidity in earthy substances,
it would entail the postulation of something unseen elsewhere to assume that very same thing— by way of identity— is the preventer of the destruction of both those properties in this case.

It should be understood that since the author of the treatise does not accept fluidity in earth (*pārthiva*), there is no need to postulate the conjunction with another substance as an obstructing factor for the destruction of its fluidity; furthermore, in this view, one must postulate an additional obstructive capacity for the [earth] itself in that case. Thus ends the section on fire (*tejas*).

The definition is: "that which exists only in what possesses a touch that is not produced by heat and is neither hot nor cold. The word "only" (*mātra*) is included to exclude earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*).

Since earth-ness subsists in an earthly atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*), which is distinct from that which possesses a touch not produced by heat and is neither hot nor cold, it is thereby excluded. Furthermore, in this context, [the definition refers to] subsisting only in that which possesses such a touch.

The factor [of exclusion] consists merely in not occurring in what is different from that which possesses such a touch; however, "occurring in that which possesses such a touch" is not also a constituent part there, because it would serve no purpose, as even *ātmatva* (the nature of self) and so forth are excluded simply by virtue of not occurring in what is different from that which possesses such a touch.

The inclusion of "direct pervasion" (*sākṣādvyāpyatva*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to [universals] such as cloth-ness (*paṭatva*); and that [direct pervasion] consists merely in not being pervaded by any genus (*jāti*) that is itself pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*), since genera residing in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are excluded by the very clause stating that they do not reside in anything other than what possesses such touch.
The term "universal" (*jāti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) resulting from the inclusion of the duality of air-cloth (*vāyupaṭadvitva*).
Although *pṛthivītva* (earthness) could be excluded by specifying that the property does not reside in anything distinct from that which possesses non-heat-produced touch (*apākajasparśavat*),
the term "possessing non-hot and non-cold touch" (*anuṣṇāśītasparśavat*) is stated because [the former specification] would fail to exclude *jalatva* (waterness) and other such properties.

Since the first [definition] involves an excess due to its being constituted by two occurrences delimited by the same locus, it is more cumbersome than the alternative definition—which is constituted by subsistence in a single locus—stated as follows: "produced by baking," etc. The term "non-occurring" (*avṛtti*) is included in order to exclude "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*).
The term "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) is included to exclude water-ness (*jalatva*).

The word "touch" (*sparśa*) is used here specifically to ensure the acquisition of the meaning "a particular universal subsumed under touch-ness (*sparśatva-vyāpya-jāti*) that qualifies the term 'neither hot nor cold' (*anuṣṇāśīta-paramāṇu*); otherwise, [the definition would be over-extensive]."
Because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) if one were to take as the genus (*jāti*) the nature of being a substratum for cognitions and so forth that are distinct due to heat and cold;

however, the term "touch" (*sparśa*) in the preceding clause is intended to secure the quality of being produced by heating (*pākajatva*) through inherence (*samavāya*), otherwise it would follow that even air (*vāyu*)—by way of temporal relation (*kālika*) and so on—would possess touch produced by heating, which is impossible. The rest is to be understood as before.

By this [statement], namely the passage beginning with "etenaitad" (by this, this), the text in the root [treatise] beginning with "vastutastu yadyapi" (but in reality, although... is intended precisely to dispel the doubt that has been shown.

Thus, we perceive it as correct that the intention of the root text is that there is no fault whatsoever if the definition of air (*vāyu*) is simply the possession of a touch distinct from other types [of touch]. 42.

Regarding the phrase "to prevent the proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhanavāraṇāya*): this is intended as a proof of being subsistent in a substance (*dravyāśritatva*) by way of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*) with the universal "tactileness" (*sparśatva*). This is because when a probandum is established by way of its own delimiting property (*avacchedakāvacchedena*), the establishment [of it] by way of co-inherence does not constitute an obstacle. The same should be understood for what follows hereafter.

Regarding the phrase "sound-series" (*śabdasantāna*): although the qualification "possessing touch" (*sparśavatva*) is redundant in the probandum because conjunction with a substance possessing velocity alone is the generator of sound—since touch is not required for the production of sound—nevertheless, by the aforementioned inference alone, [the existence] of air... [is established]. *Rāmarudrī*: By the aforementioned inference alone, [the existence] of air... [is established]. (Note: The provided source text contains a fragmentary commentary on a logical argument regarding the nature of sound and its relation to air. The translation reflects the technical philosophical context.)

It should be understood that "possessing touch" (*sparśavat*) is also included for the purpose of establishing [the probandum]; for it must be noted that a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) is not a fault when the probandum is already established. As for the claim that "possessing touch" is stated to prevent the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntaratā*)—namely, that conjunction with space (*gagana*) and so forth is the cause—it may be argued that even so, there remains the fallacy of proving something else, namely, that conjunction with fire (*tejas*) is the cause.

Because the [objection] that "it remains in that very state" is unsatisfactory, he says "possessing velocity" (*vegavat*). That is not correct; for here the term "velocity" refers to the velocity that generates the motion of a distinct substance. Thus, since velocity exists in fire (*tejas*) as well, even if it were included, there would be no fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*). And so, the inclusion of "possessing touch" (*sparśavatva*) is for the sake of [distinguishing] air (*vāyu*).
It should be understood that this is precisely for the sake of establishing contact (*sparśa*). "Not presided over by beings such as ourselves" means:
because it is the support of a substance not caused by conjunction with a self possessing volitional effort (*prayatnavad-ātma-saṃyoga*).
"The support of a boat" means: like the support of a substance situated in water. "Situated in water, etc. [refers to the aforementioned support].
And this is with the intention that the probandum (sādhya) is not intended to be established by way of its delimiting adjunct (avacchedakāvacchedena),

but rather by way of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇyena). Otherwise, even if the probandum were established in the case of grass and so forth held [by an agent] in such a manner, the establishment of the probandum would still occur only in the case of grass and so forth held by air alone.

The meaning is that there is no purpose in making the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) under the delimitation of the delimiting factor (avacchedakāvacchedena) the intended goal, because such a result would arise from the mere possibility of the establishment of air (vāyu). Regarding the phrase "in the ether" (nabhasi): its meaning is "not presided over by anything possessing touch other than air. [This is said] if the term "ether" (nabhas) were intended to mean "that which is conjoined with ether."
It should be understood that this is because it is impossible for [the Lord] to sustain grass and other things situated in water. Regarding the term "by one possessing effort" (*prayatnavat*):
the meaning is "in the sustaining of the earth and other worlds by the Supreme Lord," and not "in the sustaining of a jar and so forth by ourselves and others"—that is the intended sense.

It should be noted that there is no possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra), because the probandum— in the form of being caused by a conjunction with such a substance consisting of hands and so forth belonging to ourselves and others— is also present [in the subject]. He states the method for establishing air (*vāyu*) through action (*karman*) with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*).

The term "without" (*antareṇa*) is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the motion of grass and the like produced by the impact of an earthly object. The purpose of including "possessing touch" (*sparśavatva*) in the probandum (*sādhya*) is the same as before. Regarding action consisting of purposeful movement (*ceṣṭā*):
To exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the term "of a different kind" (*vijātīya*) is included in the definition of the probans (*hetu*). Its meaning is "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*).
In this context, distinctness consists simply in being non-motion (*ceṣṭā*) while not being produced by velocity (*vega*); it does not, however, consist in a specific universal (*jāti*).

Even if a specific universal (*jāti*) could be established in respect to effort (*ceṣṭā*)— by virtue of its being the delimitor of the effectness (*kāryatā*) as determined by the causality residing in effort, which is itself delimited by the relation of delimitingness (*avacchedakatā-saṃbandha*)— there is nonetheless a lack of evidence to establish it in the case of actions residing in insentient things. Nor...

It should not be argued that, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the establishment of distinct classes (*jātyantara*) among non-conscious actions by virtue of their being delimited by the state of being produced by the impact of a substance possessing touch, it would follow that, in the same way,
there would also be distinct classes in inference (*anumiti*) by virtue of their being delimited by the state of being produced by the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of smoke and so forth.

Because it would entail the undesirable consequence that the property of being an inference based on a mark such as smoke (*dhūmādiliṅgakānumititva*) alone must be accepted by all as the delimitor of its effecthood (*tatkāryatāvacchedaka*), making an "established conclusion" (*iṣṭāpatti*) impossible; and because, since the causal relation can be established through another method, it is inappropriate to postulate an additional universal (*jāti*).

Therefore, because the distinction between the infinite individual instances of action is difficult to discern, and because [the word] is perceived as denoting "striving" (*ceṣṭate*) due to its distinct character,
the preceding member of the compound *coṣaṭātvajāti-kāraka-stha-pūrva-pada* must, in the case of fire (*tejas*), signify that which is immediately prior [to the action].
Since permanence and so forth are not explicitly mentioned in the verse (*kārikā*), there is an apparent inconsistency; therefore, he states "like water" to clarify that meaning.
[Objection: But it was already stated [in the verse], so this is inconsistent.
Since the eternality and other properties of air have not been mentioned, he says "to be understood" (bodhyam) for that purpose.

"Of those" (teṣām) means of greed and so forth. "Being a substance conjoined [with the body]" (saṃyogidravyatvena) means being a substance conjoined with the body. [This applies] only to two substances.
The mention of its being "connected with the body" is intended to clarify that, because the hair arises from conjunction [with the body], it does not possess the nature of the body itself. Even so,

since there is an absence of the sense of touch (*tvag-indriya*) in the *purītat*— which is a specific vessel (*nāḍī*) among the bodily parts— it follows that for this reason as well, it is not [the body].

The possibility of its pervading the body is not accepted during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) because of the necessity of obstructing cognition [therein]; nevertheless, what is intended by "pervading the body" is simply its presence in all the parts of the body, and that [presence] exists even in the *purītat*.

Even in the absence of the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), this remains unimpaired by accepting that the specific central channel (*nāḍī-viśeṣa*) which generates dreams is indeed the *purītad*, because although the region of the *purītad* is a part of a channel,
it lacks the status of being a part of the body. Nor [is there a contradiction] regarding its pervading the body...
[The definition of being an organ is] precisely the state of not being the counter-positive of an absence that resides in the body and is non-co-located with its own counter-positive; thus,

even though the *purītata* is a part of the body, and even though the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*) is the counter-positive of an absence residing in the body as delimited by it, [the sense of touch is still an organ].

It should not be said that "pervasion of the body is untenable," because if that were the case, there would be no harm even if hair and the like were considered parts of the body; consequently, the authors' effort in establishing them as distinct substances would be rendered futile. However, others [argue as follows]:...

The pericardium (*purītat*) is indeed a portion of the space within the body; however, because there is no skin (*tvak*) in the [external] sky, there is an absence of cognition when the mind resides there. It is with this very intention that it was said: "O Mind, in another birth, you were always devoted to Pālita; therefore, for even a moment, direct your gaze toward the feet of Kṛṣṇa."

They say that this also accords with an ancient verse: "O mind, set out! Thus entreated, yet agitated by the fear of the destruction of its own home, it remained in the midst of sleep, neither having gone to the sky nor having reached His lotus feet."

The innate obscuration (*sahajāvaraṇa*) is the natural obscuration (*svābhāvikāvaraṇa*), which has the form of a skin. Regarding the phrase "in time and so forth" (*kālādau*): although there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time and so forth when the definition is formulated by including a producedness delimited by being tangible (*spārśanatvāvaccchinnajanyatā*), such inclusion of producedness is nevertheless necessary in the definition; otherwise, [the definition would apply] to everything that is merely produced.

In the view that time is merely an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to the eye remains as it was. Nor can it be said that during the dissolution (*pralaya*), the determination of moments, ghaṭikās, and so forth, occurs solely through action; for if that were not admitted there, it would be impossible for the durations of creation and dissolution well-known from the Purāṇas to have a single measure, since such a determination does not occur during the dissolution. *Rāmarudrī*: [This refers to the fact that] if one does not accept [the existence of time] there [during dissolution], the Purāṇic accounts of the duration of the periods of creation and dissolution could not be established by a single standard of measurement, because [the determining factor, namely action,] is absent during the dissolution.
The statement that "there is no division of space and time" refers to the context of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Thus,

even if one accepts that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) possesses the status of a temporal adjunct (*upādhi*) during the great dissolution, one must still postulate the status of being a temporal adjunct for everything else that is produced and distinct from action, beyond that [destruction].
It should not be said that this view is inconsistent due to the absence of a seed (bīja);

for if that were the case, there would be the fault of complexity (gaurava) in postulating the status of being a limiting adjunct (upādhi) for all present-day days and so forth across infinite individual actions,
whereas if everything produced were [regarded] as such, [the principle would be simpler].

Since it is possible for a single individual instance, such as a jar, that persists for only a day to possess that very nature (the capacity to produce cognition), and since parsimony (*lāghava*) itself can be the basis for that [definition], such a view is indeed consistent; nevertheless,
it should be understood that the word "sense-organ" (*indriya*) is included precisely to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as contact with the skin.

At the root, the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is conjoined with the skin; since the skin, which is of the nature of hide, serves as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the sense-faculty, he states—by supplying the word "sense-faculty"—that its meaning is "the sense-faculty situated in the skin," namely, the *tvagindriya*. Regarding the phrase "in the middle":

The sense is that, by the inclusion of the particle *eva* (only) along with that [term], only the non-manifestation of color (*rūpa*) and so forth is obtained; thus, even though the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*) manifests touch-ness (*sparśatva*), there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
This is to be understood as a qualification of the word "cognition" (*bodha*), and so forth. || 43 || [The vital breath] in the heart.

The meaning of such passages as "delimited by the heart alone" (*hṛnmātrāvaccchinna*) is as follows: if taken literally, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the *vyāna* breath would be a *prāṇa*. "Elevating" (*samunnayana*) means inflaming; the sense is that its increase occurs only through the assistance of the wind, due to its friendship with fire (*vahni*). [This is] because of the spreading of the essence of food (*annarasa*).
The meaning is "from its expansion. Thus ends the section on Air (Vāyu). Now, one might object:

at the occasion of defining space (ākāśa), it should have been stated simply that "spaceness (ākāśatva) is not a universal (jāti)," because it is more appropriate to deny the status of a universal to temporality (kālatva) and directionality (diktvatva) precisely at the occasion of defining those [time and space].

In response to the doubt—"Why is the refutation of the generic character (*jāti*) of these three being undertaken right now in the *Muktāvalī*?"—he says "kālatvam" and so forth. [This will be addressed] later, at the occasion of their respective definitions. Thus, regarding the threefold repetition of the phrase "it is not a genus" (*na jātiḥ*).
The sense is that there would be excessive prolixity in the text. The word *tat* is an indeclinable meaning "therefore.
Now, one might object that even so, the mention [of this topic] remains disconnected;
to this he says: "on account of the connection with another" (*para-saṅgāt*). "Connection" (*prasaṅga*) means the state of being unfit to be neglected once it has been brought to mind.
The intended meaning is that those two [ākāśa and ātman] are also remembered as objects inferred from a single cause.
Thus, it should be understood that because they are mentioned here by way of a contextual transition (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*), there is no fallacy of shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*).
In the root text, the phrase "because space and so forth consist of a single individual" [is stated] on account of the absence of generic character (*jāti*) in *ākāśatva* and the like.

The reason has been stated; having raised the objection that the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) reside in different loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), he completes the reason with the word "aneka" (many). Although the connection is as follows: "Even though [properties] such as 'space-ness' (*ākāśatva*) in space and so forth are not universals (*jāti*) because they belong to only a single individual (*ekavyaktikatvāt*)," in that case, the term *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of "that which has only one individual as its locus."

The suffix *kapratyaya* [denotes] "thatness" (*tattva*), meaning "the state of being that. The meaning is as follows: in the substratum (*āśraya*), there is unity (*ekatva*) which consists in being other than that which is qualified by difference through two relations: (1) possessing an adventitious property (*upādhi*) that is a differentiator of substance (*dravyavibhājaka*) residing in its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogin*), and (2) being the substratum itself (*svāśrayatva*). An object such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) possesses such a qualification, but space (*ākāśa*) and the like do not.

"Having that as its substratum" (tadāśrayakatva) means, in short, "having that as its locus. Although the reason stated in the root-text could be refined in this manner, nevertheless, considering the complexity (gaurava) of such a reason, the reason is formulated as the absence of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) of a conjunction (samavāya) that has multiple relata (anekānuyogika).

It is fulfilled. Multiplicity (*anekatva*) is not a number distinct from unity; for if that were the case, since qualities are not admitted to possess further qualities, there would exist—in the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatva-jāti*) as well—the absence of being the counter-positive of an inherence whose relatum possesses such a number.

Because [if it were defined otherwise] there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*); rather, it is the state of being the object of a particular enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). And although this is non-uniform because enumerative cognitions themselves are non-uniform, it is nevertheless the absence of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an inherence (*samavāya*) that has as its relatum (*anuyogika*) the object of some single individual instance of cognition.

The status of being a cause by virtue of the commonality of universals such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is impossible to maintain; nevertheless, there is no fault, because the intended meaning is "being other than that which is qualified by difference" through the two relations of "inherence in its own counter-correlative" and "inherence in its own locus. Even by this much...
This is because there is no loss of parsimony (*lāghava*) compared to the previously stated reason consisting of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that differentiates substances.
Furthermore, one should not suspect that, due to parsimony, the absence of inherence (*samavetatvābhāva*) alone is the appropriate reason;
for, by parsimony relative to being the inherent cause of sound (*śabda-samavāyikāraṇatva*), sound itself is the nature of space (*ākāśatva*).

It should be noted that this would result in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "vaiyadhikaraṇyamiti" (the lack of common locus):
this is based on the etymological derivation that *ekavyaktika* means "that which has only one individual instance," and its state (*tattva*) is "the fact of having only one individual instance";
thus, it results in the meaning "because of having only one individual instance," as stated in the root text (*mūla*). And in that case...

Since even *dravyatva* (substance-ness) and the like would entail the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by virtue of being instantiated in only a single individual, it was stated with the intention that [the phrase] "because space and so forth consist of a single individual" is to be construed with [the reason] "because they consist of a single individual"; for if the meaning were as previously stated, there would be no lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Nor is this the case now.

It should not be said that the statement in the root text is redundant because the reason "because there is only one individual possessing such a meaning" could possibly serve as the logical ground; for the intention is that it was introduced precisely as a means of establishing the reason. And as for the phrase "in this way": [it refers to] the term *vaiśeṣika* [applying] to space (*ākāśa*).

The meaning is: "when it has the purpose of excluding other specific qualities. "With restriction" means "accompanied by the particle *eva*," as in "sound alone. The intention is that only when this is the case is it possible to obtain the stated meaning. "Being a specific quality... [and so forth].
The sense is that immediately after the specific quality-ness (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) has been established in sound,

the reason for proving ether (*ākāśa*), which will be stated later, can be established in sound according to the method to be described. The phrase "of the nature of demonstrating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding ether" refers to this.

Regarding the phrase "in a jar, etc.": the meaning of the second part of the definition is that [the universal] such as *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness) is the object of a common-sense perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) produced by the sense of touch (*tvag-indriya*).
In the case of the statement "the jar is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the word," it refers to the aspect of the word.

The inclusion of the term "extraordinary" (*alaukika*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*), since sound is also inherently capable of being the object of an extraordinary visual perception;
had one merely stated that it is not the object of such a perception, [the argument would fail] due to the absence of visual contact (*cakṣussaṃyoga*) and other such conditions.

Since the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was in the case of jars and the like—which are not objects of such perception—the inclusion of "essential capacity" (*svarūpayogyatā*) is necessary. And that [capacity] belongs only to those things enumerated in such passages as, "Manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the object of the eye," and so forth. This is the sense. [The phrase] "grasped by an external sense organ" (*bahirindriyagrāhya*)...

The state of being graspable by an external sense organ (*bahirindriyagrāhyatva*) consists in being the object of a worldly direct perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) produced by an external sense organ. The inclusion of the term "worldly" (*laukika*) is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the self (*ātman*).
Now, since the genus "substance-ness" (*dravyatvajāti*) and others—which are graspable by an external sense organ—exist in the self, the deviation remains unavoidable. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that the qualification "ending in -sat" (real) applies only to the genus (*jāti*), and thus, since the property of substantiality (*dravyatva*) is not perceptible by the eye, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the self (*ātman*) when that [property] is taken as the subject;
for if that were the case, it would be sufficient simply to state that [the genus] is not an object of visual perception (*cākṣuṣāviṣayatva*).
If it is argued that there is no need to include the qualification of "specific fitness" (yogyatāviśeṣa),
because there is no evidence for a genus (*jāti*) residing in qualities (*guṇa*) that are objects of the visual sense and are perceivable by external senses—
and thus no possibility of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurring by taking such a genus as the locus— then this is not so.

Since the reason "because it possesses a genus (jāti) that is perceptible by an external sense organ" has the meaning "because, while being perceptible by an external sense organ, it possesses a genus," there is no possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the self (ātman);

furthermore, the inclusion of "possessing a genus" is meaningful precisely for the purpose of avoiding deviation in cases such as the destruction (dhvaṃsa) of sound. It is not [the case that this is redundant].
Nor should it be said that there is thus a fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*); for since sound is possible as something not perceptible by the external senses,

the existence of ether (*ākāśa*) can be established through the subsistence [of sound] in a substance other than the eight substances, by way of its co-inherence with the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*).

Since there is no purpose in proving "quality-ness" (guṇatva) as delimited by "sound-ness" (śabdatva), the intended object of proof is the establishment of quality-ness through co-inherence (sāmānādhikaraṇya); and when the establishment of the probandum through co-inherence is the intended object, partial non-pervasion (bhāgāsiddhi) is not a defect.
The meaning is: "for the sake of knowing the absence of the probans in 'rasatva' (the nature of being taste) and so forth, in order to exclude [the probans] from 'rasatva' and the like.

The point is that otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of *rasatva*—which is graspable by the gustatory organ but not graspable by the visual organ—due to the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*). This applies to sound as well.
He shows the utility of the inference regarding "being a genus" (*gaṇatva*) for the subject at hand with the words "And this.
He states the result of the inference regarding "inherence in a substance" (*dravyasamavetatva*) with the words "By means of this inference.
Inference based on a general reason (*sāmānyahetu*) assisted by the absence of specific [alternatives] is *pariśeṣānumāna* (inference by elimination).

In the proof that "it is not a quality of a specific substance possessing touch," once the absence of being a quality of any specific substance such as earth is established, there is no establishment of the absence of being a quality of a specific substance in general that possesses touch, which was the intended object of proof; therefore...

He explains this with the words "not of that which possesses touch," and so forth. If the reason is formulated as "because it is the object of a perception that, while not being produced by cooking (apākaja), is not preceded by the qualities of its cause," there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of color and other qualities that are preceded by the qualities of their causes; furthermore, [the reason would fail] in the case of the self, because of the absence of a cause for it.
Since perception alone does not necessarily have qualities of its causes as its antecedents, he says "not preceded by the qualities of its causes" (akāraṇa) for that purpose.

Regarding the phrase "produced by baking" (pākaja): by the very mention of being produced by baking, the exclusion of being generated by the qualities of its causes is obtained; thus, [the definition applies] when it is not preceded by the qualities of its causes.

The sense is that there is the possibility of apprehending the reason consisting in the nature of being perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*). Regarding the phrase "neglect here": "here" refers to the demonstration of the exclusion [of the definition] by the component "perceptibility"; "neglect" means their non-apprehension. The meaning is: because those [objects] are perceptible, they are objects of the perception produced by that [perception]. [Thus,] it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If sound were a common quality (sāmānyaguṇa), there would follow the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the qualification "not residing in the eight substances"; furthermore, since there is deviation in the case of conjunction produced by action and so forth, it is impossible to prove that sound is distinct from qualities possessing touch by means of the stated reason.

The sense is that in establishing the distinction from the specific qualities of tangible substances, there is the possibility of [those qualities] being general qualities of tangible substances. Regarding the phrase "by means of ordinary sensory contact" (*laukikapratyāsatti*): this is stated with reference to the fact that even properties such as gravity (*gurutva*) are perceptible by the senses through the contact of the "presentation" (*upanaya*).

To exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the second such term is also for the very purpose of excluding non-establishment (*asiddhi*), since sound and touch would otherwise be perceptible by the eye through the contact of the "bringing forward" (*upanaya*).
Regarding the phrase "by two sense organs": it refers to the capacity for apprehension by those respective sense organs within the genus (*jāti*).
Therefore, the term "perceivable by two sense organs" (*dvīndriya*) should be understood as referring to a state of being perceptible by two *heterogeneous* sense organs;

otherwise, since even color and other qualities are capable of being grasped by two eyes, it would be impossible to establish anything that is not "perceivable by two sense organs. Although... [Rāmarudrī]... [text continues].

It would be more appropriate to state that for all universals (jāti), such as number and the rest, "while not being perceptible by two sense organs" means they are perceptible by two sense organs at different times and in different persons;
for there is no purpose in introducing the notion of "capacity" (yogyatā). Nevertheless, regarding the property of being produced by two sense organs...
It was not stated in that way because it would result in the fallacy of non-establishment due to its impossibility in some cases.

Nor should it be argued that "being perceptible by two senses" cannot be defined as a uniform property consisting of being qualified by a sense-organ through the two relations of being the object of a cognition produced by a sense-organ whose essence is itself, and being the object of a cognition produced by a sense-organ of a different class from itself.
This is because the intention is that this [definition] is excessively cumbersome due to the inclusion of "being produced" (*janyatva*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that even in the view where "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is included, the fitness of the sense organ is nothing other than its residing in an object of ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) produced by that [sense organ], and thus the property of being a locus (*ādheyatva*) is merely superfluous.
Visual fitness consists in being any one of the manifested colors and so forth;
tactile fitness consists in being any one of the manifested tangibles and so forth, since such is the nature of sensory fitness.
And "being any one" is the absence of the collection of differences [from all others], and that [absence] exists only by virtue of each specific individuality (*tattad-vyaktitvena*).
It should be understood that there is no loss of parsimony (*lāghava*) by accepting [the property] as being included within the definition of fitness (*yogyatā*).

Regarding the term "inherent" (*sāṃsiddhika*): the meaning is that because the generic properties of such fluidity (*dravatvatva*) and viscidity (*snehatva*) are perceptible by the skin and the eye, whereas merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) are supersensible (*atīndriya*), the probans does not exist in those latter cases. Regarding the phrase "by another probans alone": these five...

The inference should be understood as follows: "The specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇas) [are such] because, while being distinct from the quality of elasticity (sthitisthāpaka), they possess a genus that is pervaded by the category of quality (guṇatva) and is not delimited by the subsistence in two individual instances characterized by a property that divides substances. This is with respect to the previously mentioned inference.

In the inference where the probandum is the absence of being a specific quality of that which possesses touch (*sparśavat-viśeṣaguṇatvābhāva*), the phrase "for the purpose of demonstrating the unestablished nature of the reason" refers to the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth. Regarding the word "of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaḥ*):
it is stated to be a valid cognition because of the visual error "the sky is blue. [Verse 44] Regarding the phrase "excessive prolixity" (*atigaurava*).
The sense is that, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), there would result the assumption of sound as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) in multiple living beings,
as well as the postulation of an additional relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*). Nor [can this be avoided] by taking time and space [as the locus].

It should not be said that there is a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*), for it should be understood that even those two are included within Īśvara himself by the moderns (*navīnas*). Now, according to the independent system (*svatantramata*), the sense organ that perceives sound is—

What is its nature? It is precisely the nature of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). Even if the ear were the mere cavity, there would be no need for an additional postulation [of the auditory organ], because according to all schools of thought, it is necessary to postulate that a defect residing in the body acts as an obstacle to the perception of sound in order to prevent a deaf person from perceiving sound.
Thus, there is no excess of such postulation in the view that the cavity alone is the sense-organ.
If it is asked, "What then is the contact of the ear with the sound inherent in a drum?

and if it is replied, "It is inherence in that which is conjoined with what is conjoined with itself," [we respond]: No, because that would involve the conceptual complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating yet another contact. It is not so; for [the contact] is simply that very self.

Because it is admitted to be the auditory sense-organ (*śrotrendriya*) belonging to that [self]. Nor should it be asked how this is possible given the contradiction between being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and being an instrument (*karaṇatva*); for just as in the case of "he knows himself" (*svātmānaṃ vetti*), where there is no contradiction between being an agent and being an object (*karmatva*), so too there is no contradiction here. And thus, by not postulating mere inherence (*samavāya*) as a means of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*).

There is also another [instance of] parsimony (*lāghava*). Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of perceiving sound even during the state when the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*) is covered;
for even on the view that such [covered] space is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), there is no obstacle to the production of sound in space that is obstructed by some object. Therefore, its...

Since the postulation of its being an obstacle to perception is necessary even in the established doctrine (siddhānta), such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the section on space (ākāśa). Regarding the general category of effects, since it is impossible for time to be an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) and also impossible for it to be a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)...

Since [the term] is not applicable to a substance (*dravya*), he explains the word "producer" (*janaka*) as referring to an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), stating: "the meaning is 'efficient cause'. Since the phrase "the substratum of the worlds" (*jagatām āśrayaḥ*) in the root text is to be explained as having the purpose of demonstrating the proof for time (*kāla*), [he provides the commentary] beginning with "of produced things" (*janyānām*).
It must be stated that [the text] is solely intended to demonstrate the definition of time,

because the meaning of the word "nirūpaṇa" (demonstration) is precisely the statement of the definition, the means of valid cognition, and the essential nature [of the object]; and that [statement] is not possible even for space and so forth with respect to the general category of effects.
Because there would be an over-extension [of the definition] if it were taken as an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), he says: "In this case.

"By way of being a locus" (*adhikaraṇavidhayā*) means by way of being a substratum (*adhikaraṇatvena*). Although it is more appropriate that time is the cause of every effect solely by virtue of its nature as time, rather than by virtue of being a substratum—[this is the objection].
Since it is impossible for [space] and the like to serve as delimiters (avacchedaka) for the causal power residing in time due to their over-extension (atiprasaktatva),

and since "time-ness" (kālatva) cannot be a universal (jāti) because it consists of only a single individual, and furthermore, because it is impossible to define "time-ness" as anything other than the state of being a locus (adhikaraṇatva) delimited by the temporal relation (kālika-sambandha), it is stated [in the text] that it functions "as a locus. Thus, [it is concluded in] the Rāmarudrī.

Some maintain that there is no inconsistency because the "time-ness" (*niruktakālatva*) consists in the nature of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*); likewise, "direction-ness" (*dik-tva*) is also nothing but the state of being a locus by virtue of being a qualifier produced by direction. Therefore, they argue, there is no inconsistency in stating that the definition over-extends to direction (*diś*). This is incorrect; for if that were the case, [the definition] would apply to the definition of Great Time (*mahākāla*).

Because over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would occur in the case of a jar and other such things, and since the proof for that very point will be demonstrated later, it is determined that only that [the self] is the subject of the definition (*lakṣya*). However, the meaning is simply "by way of the relation of identity" (*tādātmya-sambandhena*), because the substratum is everywhere the cause precisely by that [relation]. Being an instrumental cause (*nimittatva*) means being a cause (*kāraṇatva*), and not—

It should be understood that [space] possesses the nature of an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) because there is no purpose for its inclusion [as an inherent cause].
