The phrase "in the case of space" is to be construed with what follows, namely, that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti). In the expression "of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) and God (īśvara)," the mention of God is intended to convey that He is the cause solely as an agent (kartṛ) in respect of every effect. However, according to the view that agency is the causal factor...

The term "īśvara-pada" (the word "Lord") should be understood as referring to His creative activity. Regarding the phrase "as the locus of origination": the sense is that, in the present context, the verbal root *bhū* signifies "origination.
Regarding the phrase "of the object of conventional usage": this refers to instances such as "a jar originates in the pot-sherd," and so forth.

The meaning is "because of being perceived. Although the shards and so forth do not possess the status of being the direct locus (*sākṣād-ādhāra*) for the production of a jar, nevertheless, as in expressions such as "he cooks in the house," their status as such should be understood through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*). Although production, which consists in a relation to the first moment, is essentially nothing other than the action (*kriyā*) characterized by those respective qualifiers.
Since the temporal relation having such a moment as its relatum is identical with the nature of that very moment,
the causality of such a moment [with respect to] those respective days and so forth is indeed subject to dispute;
furthermore, the example of the potsherd and so forth is entirely untenable, and the aforementioned rule is also unestablished as it lacks probative force.
Even so, it is precisely one who is perceived as the substratum of origination (*utpatti*) that is accepted as the cause;
thus, since the admission of such a restriction is possible, there is no purpose whatsoever in including "origination" (*utpatti*) [in the definition].
However, it is solely for the sake of preventing the contingency of origination being accidental (*ākasmikatva*) that "origination" is included in the restriction.

If, by virtue of being included [in that category], those [actions] were essentially of the nature of action and so forth, then—since they would be governed by their own respective causes—they would not incur the consequence of being accidental; thus, their inclusion [in that category] would be entirely redundant. And likewise, in the case of mango fruits and the like which are restricted to specific times, the causality of specific time is necessarily required.

We consider it highly appropriate that, according to the Nyāya principle "that which [is the cause] of two particulars," the causality of time with respect to the generality of effects is established;
it is precisely with this intention that the word "they say" (āhuḥ) was used to indicate a lack of final satisfaction. And as for "that" (sā ca):
The meaning is that, according to the method stated, the other two causes are impossible at the time [of the perception].
It has been established in the root-text (*mūla*) that cognitions such as "now" have as their objects the solar motion (*parispanda*) and so forth.

He introduces this with the words "Now," etc. [The phrase] "because of the consequence that there would be no cognition" means that the Great Time (*mahākāla*) is the substratum of all things; this is the intended sense. Although the cognition "the jar is not at that time" alone possesses a sublated object, the cognition "the jar is now" does not.

If one were to argue that the component "now" (idānīm) is not useful in the present context, yet—unlike space and so forth—time is not the locus of anything by means of a temporal relation, and therefore the expression "the jar at that time" (tadānīm ghaṭaḥ) is not untenable, then [we reply] that even the expression "the jar now" (idānīm ghaṭaḥ) would likewise not be possible. *Rāmarudrī:* [This is the commentary on the above. If one were to say: "The part 'now' has no utility here; however, since time—unlike space—is not the locus of any entity through a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), the expression 'the jar at that time' is not logically inconsistent. To this we reply: if that were so, then the expression "the jar now" (*idānīm ghaṭaḥ*) would also be impossible. This is because, according to that view, there could be no such thing as a temporal relation between the jar and the time "now. Thus, the objection fails.

It should be understood that the mention of that [ether] is for the purpose of making it known; "only ether" means that the intention is that even by taking ether, a series of relations consisting of conjunctions with what is conjoined to its own substratum can be established. "Because of being such" means because of being a constituent of the relation.
Although space and the like function as constituents of a relation solely by virtue of being their own conjuncts—

and not by virtue of properties such as "spatiality" (ākāśatva)— there is no room for an objection regarding a lack of a decisive criterion; for it is indeed accepted that all pervasive entities, established as such in that form, serve as constituents of relations.

Because there is no decisive reason [to prefer one over the other]. Nor should it be argued that, rather than postulating such an infinite series as comprising the constituent members of that succession for infinite individuals, it is simpler (laghu) to postulate only one additional individual; for [otherwise] time would not serve as a constituent of the conjunction between the conjoined entities.

This [definition] is inconsistent because, in the absence of a specific qualifier that excludes space (*ākāśa*) and so forth which are conjoined with itself, it would be unavoidable [to over-extend]; nevertheless, an infinite number of individual conjunctions with space and so forth must be postulated for the pot, as there is no decisive reason (*avinigamana*) to restrict its relational status to any one of them.
However, if one were to postulate a distinct entity called "time," that postulation would apply only to its conjunction [with objects]; thus, there is parsimony (lāghava).

As has already been explained, it is impossible for there to be no restriction (avaniyamana) toward the conjunction with unestablished time when one can instead adopt the conjunction with established entities such as space (ākāśa).

The intended meaning (tātparya) should be understood as follows: regarding the phrase "an additional substance called time" (*atiriktakāla*), if a substance named time existed as something distinct [from the other categories], it would be untenable for the aforementioned cognition to have space (*dik*) as its object, because space is not mentioned therein. Furthermore, the word "time" (*kāla*) cannot denote the sense of "space" (*dik*) without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, if one were to accept such a distinct substance, it would entail the abandonment of the primary meaning of the term.

The state [of being]. || 45 || In the root text, it is not possible for "the uncommon cause" (*asādhāraṇaṃ nimittam*) to mean "the instrumental cause with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of such a cognition," because there is no evidence for such a causal status; therefore, the word *pada* must be taken in the sense of "that which prompts" (*prayojaka*).
He clarifies this with the passage beginning with "the elder" and ending with "the state. Regarding the phrase "the means of knowledge":
the establishment of temporal priority and posteriority occurs through the very cognition of distinctness—such as "Rāma is the elder, Lakṣmaṇa is the younger"—for such a cognition [is the proof].
The meaning is that it is impossible for [the cognition] to have as its object "priority" (paratva) and so forth produced by spatial direction (dik).
— Rāmarudrī.

Since the object is a cause of perception, it should be understood that whatever necessitates the object also necessitates its perception. As for the claim "because of deviation": although there is no deviation regarding the posteriority of air and so forth when touch is the cause, there is nevertheless deviation with respect to number and other qualities.

The sense is that, due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), it would follow that all infinite qualities would likewise possess that nature; therefore, it is more appropriate that the conjunction with time (*kālasaṃyoga*) alone possesses that nature. "By that nature" means by being the substratum of the aforementioned non-inherent cause-conjunction (*asamavāyikāraṇasaṃyoga*). "Contradictory" (*viruddha*)... [text continues].

The contradiction pertaining to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consists precisely in the failure to convey [two properties] as delimited by a single property. The phrase "for not" (*na hi*) indicates that the statement regarding the non-contradiction of jarhood and so forth is intended solely to resolve the contradiction consisting in the failure to convey [them] as delimited by a single property within linguistic usage.
This should be understood to apply to subsequent cases as well. The word "contradictory" (*viruddha*) follows immediately after "in one" (*ekasmin*).

[The word] "pūraṇīyam" (to be supplied) [is used] because of the reasoning already stated. Regarding the phrase "draṣṭavyam" (should be seen): this is not approved by the author of the root-text (*mūlakāra*); for if that were the case, one would have to accept that the cognition of substratumhood (*ādhāratā*) regarding adjuncts (*upādhi*) occurs only through a transitive relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) involving time, which would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

It should be noted that the direct admission of [the action] as the locus is beset by the complexity resulting from the postulation of the relation of temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*) between each individual instance and the referent of the word ending in *-anta*.
Regarding the term "virukta" (unmanifested): it means the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the disjunction produced by itself.

Regarding the phrase "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*): although it is possible to define a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) during the second, third, and fourth moments even without the arising of another action, the term "at every moment" is stated because the fifth-moment condition (*pañcamakṣaṇopādhi*) can only be established through the arising of another action. Regarding the phrase "produced by itself" (*svajanya*): the word "self" (*sva*)...

The phrase "referring to the manifestation of that prior action" is intended to exclude other actions. He states the purpose of including the condition "being destructible by the disjunction produced by itself" with the words "by that [condition].

Regarding the expression "three moments": this is based on the intention that, in every case, the destruction of the disjunction occurs in the fourth moment through conjunction with a subsequent location. Otherwise, [the definition would fail] in the case of a disjunction residing in space and so forth.

The sense is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of its being non-perishable, like destruction (dhvaṃsa) and so forth. The connection with what follows is that even if it exists for three moments, there is no deficiency. He states the purpose of including "being produced by itself" (*svajanyatva*) in the definition of disjunction (*vibhāga*)—namely, "whatever..."—even though [the property of being produced by itself] is already established.
"Even though it exists for three moments, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

This means that the aforementioned over-extension— which would occur if [the definition] did not include "being produced by a disjunction generated by itself" in the case of the destruction of the prior conjunction, or if it did not include "being produced by itself" in the case of the subsequent conjunction— does not apply here.

He provides the summary: [Objection] But surely, since both conditions are possible in the third moment, there would be a deficiency if only one were mentioned; therefore, both have been stated. In the other case, however, only one condition exists at a time, so only one was mentioned. It is not by that much [that the objection stands].

To avoid the contradiction with the context, he says: "by the subsequent," etc. By the word "only" (eva), there is an exclusion of the destruction of the prior conjunction. Thus, the meaning is that even at the moment of the production of the subsequent conjunction, the disjunction indeed persists. [The phrase] "its own destroyer," etc. [is explained as follows].
The point is that even at the moment of the production of the subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*), the disjunction (*vibhāga*) still persists.

Regarding the phrase "its own destroyer" (*svanāśaka*): this was stated for the sake of understanding that the action (*kriyā*) does not persist after the subsequent conjunction; however, it would have been more appropriate to state simply "produced by itself" (*svajanyatva*) for the sake of brevity. Nor is it the case that...

It must be stated that it is precisely the destruction of the prior conjunction that produces the subsequent conjunction; for if that were not the case, it would follow that such a conjunction could arise even when the action has ceased,
and this would contradict the sūtra which defines action as "the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction."

"Of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*) means: an action delimited by the prior non-existence of disjunction (*vibhāga-prāgabhāva*), and so forth. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that [the definition] applies because the prior non-existence of subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga-prāgabhāva*), and so on, is likewise absent [in the case of the first moment]. "The locus of that" (*tad-adhikaraṇa*): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the object about to be produced; and "being the locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*) as well as the two types of "being the contained" (*ādheyatā*) are related by way of time (*kālika*).

because of the acceptance of the causal relation between experience and recollection. And thus:

The meaning is that there is one causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) by way of being the object (viṣayatā) and another by way of inherence (samavāya). However, this is merely superficial; for even if one does not accept two such causal relations according to the aforementioned method, it would follow that a recollection having "pot-ness" as its qualifier (prakāra) could arise even from an indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka) whose objects are the pot, pot-ness, and inherence.

Nor should it be argued that this fault does not apply because one accepts three distinct causal relations based on the mode-ness (*prakāratva*), object-ness (*viśeṣyatva*), and relational object-ness (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*) [of the respective cognitions], since such object-nesses are not admitted for indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). For even so, by means of "pot-ness" and "cloth-ness"...
Otherwise, from an experience having cloth as its object, there would result the recollection of a cloth having "cloth-ness" as its qualifier and "pot-ness" as its qualifier;

and from an experience having "pot-ness" as its qualifier— by way of temporal relation (*kālika*)— there would result [the recollection] of a pot having "pot-ness" as its qualifier by way of inherence (*samavāya*), [and similarly] from an experience having "cloth-ness" as its qualifier by way of inherence, [there would result the recollection] of a cloth having "cloth-ness" as its qualifier by way of inherence.

Since it is impossible to avoid the consequence that there would be a recollection having "cloth" as its qualificandum and "clothness" as its qualifier by means of a causal relation (*kālika*), one must, as a last resort, hold that the experience has "pot" as its qualificandum, "potness" as its qualifier, and "inherence" (*samavāya*) as its relation; and the recollection likewise has "pot" as its qualificandum, "potness" as its qualifier, and "inherence" as its relation.

Because it must be postulated. However, if one accepts a causal relationship between remembrance and experience based on the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as constituted by the relation of temporal qualification (*kālika-viśeṣaṇatā-pratyāsatti*), then [the objection that] what was experienced by one sense organ... [Rāmarudrī].

Since recollection can also occur through another sense organ, the expression "by means of the proximity of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-pratyāsatti*)"— which signifies a co-referentiality constituted by inherence (*samavāya*)— is stated in the root text.

We consider this to be logical. (Verse 48) [The objection] "there would be a lack of connection" means that the mind cannot possibly be of the nature of cognition. The meaning is that [this will be] established.
Although, even if one were to accept that largeness (*mahattva*) is a cause only for mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) other than [the aforementioned], this...
This is a fault. For this very reason, although the Mādhvas and others accept that individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed atomic (*aṇu*),

nevertheless, because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the qualifier-qualified relationship between "being distinct from the mind" and "being perceptible," it results in the undesirable consequence of two excessively cumbersome causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Because of the resulting complexity, such an admission is not possible. Nor should it be argued that, according to the Siddhāntin’s view, there is no complexity in postulating two types of causality since an infinite number of souls must be postulated;
for the complexity of postulating multiple souls is not a fault, as it is "phalamukha" (incidental to the result).

[This is] the state of being. In the investigation of the doctrine that consciousness is the self, he shows the disagreement regarding its constituent parts with the words "herein. Regarding the phrase "or of existence" (*sattvasya vā*): the sense is that, according to their [the Vaiśeṣikas'] view, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are unreal (*alīka*). Here, "existence" (*sattva*) should be understood simply as the state of being connected with time. [The example is] "I know."

The meaning is "cognition having the form 'I'. By this, there is no contradiction with the continuity of the stream of *layavijñāna* (dissolution-consciousness) which will be described later during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Otherwise, since there is an absence of active cognition at that time, even in the cognition having the form "I know," there would be only active cognitions such as "pot," "cloth," and so forth.
Because it would follow that the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) could not persist at that time as its object,

and because in a cognition having the form "I," the self itself is the object; furthermore, it should be understood that a cognition such as "this is a jar" is an *active cognition* (*pravṛttijñāna*), since it serves as the means for initiating activity directed toward that object.
"Due to the absence of a cause for its arising"—
this means due to the absence of the cause consisting of the contact of the mind with a location distinct from the *purītad*.
In the root text, "in deep sleep" (*suṣuptau*) refers to that time when that *ālayavijñāna* [is present].
The sense is that even if one accepts that [consciousness] has only itself as its object, it would follow that it must appear at this time [as yellow].

"Even in the absence of a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇābhāve) means even in the absence of that which pervades the nature of being a cognition whose essence is the state of being an object-possessor (viṣayitā). "Non-different from that" (tadabhinnā) refers to the aspect of yellow, which is non-different from the consciousness whose essence is the aspect of the form of blue. (Rāmarudrī)

The meaning is that there is a rule of non-difference from blue. "Coexistence in one place" means determination as residing in a single locus. By this, even in the case of things residing in a single locus, there is no inconsistency even when there is a determination of contradiction consisting of error at a time when they are not perceived as such. [This is] by means of the material cause (*upādāna*).

In this context, "being the material cause" (upādānatva) does not mean being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva), because it is impossible for one momentary cognitive instance to be the aforementioned inherent cause of another instance occurring at a different time. Nor, according to that school's view, does it mean being its own instrument (svakaraṇatva).

According to that view, *upādānatva* (the state of being a material cause) consists in being the counter-positive of a destruction that arises at the same time as one's own arising; however, since for that school every entity whatsoever is its own cause, this definition fails because it is untenable for earlier individual jars and the like to be the material causes of subsequent individual jars and the like. This is because, even in their system, they must admit a relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) in those cases, which would result in an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

However, the material cause (*upādāna*) is that which acts without auxiliary causes (*asahakṛta*); since they accept that for a subsequent individual (*vyakti*), the preceding individual alone is the cause, the preceding individual possesses the status of a material cause with respect to the subsequent individual. Furthermore, a mother is not a cause without auxiliary factors with respect to her son.

It should be understood that even semen, blood, and so forth are causes of a son. Regarding the phrase "a specific capacity" (śaktiviśeṣa), the intended meaning is as follows: although there is the complexity of postulating a distinct individual instance of a latent impression (saṃskāra) for every individual cognition when those cognitions are held to produce latent impressions, [nevertheless], following a particular instance of cognition...

Remembrance is established by experience; therefore, one must admit a certain potency residing in a cognition that is conducive to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within that specific instance of prior cognition, rather than postulating an excellence (*atiśaya*) in every instance of cognition. Consequently, there is no infinite regress of impressions. [The term] "momentary" refers to the fact that, according to that school's view, every entity is momentary.

If one were to argue that even though [cognitions] are momentary, since the recollection of a particular object at a particular time is established by experience, one should postulate only a single power (*śakti*) within those cognitions— and thus there is no burden of postulating infinite powers— then one must instead admit that the power is indeed distinct for each individual instance of cognition (*jñānavyakti*), as is the case with all entities.

In that view, the mention of "momentariness" (kṣaṇikatvāt) is a restatement of momentariness— which is common to all categories of entities— in order to indicate the solution [to the problem of causal efficiency]; for this very reason,
it is intended to highlight that even antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destruction (dhvaṃsa) must necessarily be postulated.

The inclusion of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is also consistent [with this view]. However, the term "infinite" (*ananta*) is intended to suggest the cumbersome complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating an infinite number of individual instances; the sense is that whenever a recollection or experience occurs, it becomes necessary to postulate a distinct instance of the capacity (*śakti*).

This is an illustration. It should be understood that there is also complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the causality of individual instances of prior cognitions with respect to each respective excellence (*atiśaya*). And here, in order to dispel the doubt that—even if one were to postulate various powers—there would be no fault according to the maxim "complexity is not a defect when it is supported by authoritative evidence" (*prāmāṇika*), [the author] says: *rāmarudrī*.

The statement "because of the recognition of non-difference as 'this is that'" intends to convey that since non-difference itself is established by experience, the postulation of multiple distinct individuals is not authoritative. In reality, however, this is the reason for not accepting momentariness even for all categories of entities (*padārtha*); and thus:

In response to the objection that for those who accept momentary entities (*kṣaṇika-padārtha*), the very complexity of postulating multiple individual instances (*vyakti*) is intended as the reason [for their theory], and that in that case, "philosophical weight" (*prāmāṇika gaurava*) is not a fault, he says: "This is that very same [thing]. Thus, it is precisely non-difference (*abheda*) [that is established].
The point is that since this is established by direct experience (*anubhava*), where is there room for questioning the epistemic validity (*prāmāṇikatā*) of distinct individuals?

By this, the objection— that because perceptual cognition is of the nature of perception and powers (*śakti*) are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), recognition having them as its object is impossible— is also refuted.
"Specific universal" (*jāti-viśeṣa*) means a universal that resides in each individual seed-moment capable of producing a sprout.
Furthermore, this [universal] is of the nature of *apoha* (exclusion), because in that philosophical system, any purely inclusive property (*anugata-dharma*) is considered unreal.
"Non-acceptance of such pervasion (vyāpti)":
the sense is that *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) alone is the motivator for the aforementioned pervasion. "In my view": and thus...

The meaning is that although all things possess causality by virtue of their "producing nature" (*kurvadrūpa*), in your view, multiple distinct causalities must be postulated, which constitutes a complexity (*gaurava*). Regarding the phrase "such complexity": it means the complexity of having to postulate only a few causalities [as opposed to many].

"Because it is from the perspective of the result. This means that, rather than postulating multiple causal factors, when a single causality is established as "kurvadrūpa" (the state of performing the action) due to parsimony, and various individual instances are postulated for the sake of explaining this [causality], such a postulation occurs subsequent to the establishment of the causality; therefore, the knowledge of such complexity [would be irrelevant].
The sense is that it is impossible for there to be an obstruction to the previous inference.

Nor should it be argued that even prior to the ascertainment of the causal relation, the postulation of various individual instances is indeed established by means of the pervasion (vyāpti) expressed as "whatever exists... and so forth.

This is because, in order to dispel the suspicion that such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not probative, one must rely on the aforementioned reasoning (*tarka*); and since, in that context, a single uniform certainty that establishes the ascertainment of the absence of the probandum (*apādyavyatireka-niścaya*) is required, the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) applies, as it is more economical than the establishment of causality (*kāraṇatā*). Thus, there is a rule of priority for the latter.
The state [of being a defect]. "Because it is a defect" means that even when an inference has already arisen, a subsequent cognition of complexity (gaurava) gives rise to a cognition of invalidity;
thus, because the inference is overwhelmed by a cognition of invalidity, it is impossible for it to establish a single causal capacity.

[This is] the state of being. Although, according to that school's view, because universals (jāti) are unreal and thus lack existence, there is no momentariness [of them], since they do not admit eternal categories and do not admit any inclusive property (anugata-dharma), even the "productive nature" (kurvadrūpatva) is of the nature of an exclusion (apoha). [Rāmarudrī: And if that is so, then [there is no relation] between the existent and the non-existent...

It should not be argued that because there is no connection [between the two states], the jar lacks the property of belonging to that same class, and thus recognition is untenable; for since they admit that even a non-existent thing can appear [in cognition], the possibility of recognition remains. Nevertheless, [the objection] holds on the grounds that [recognition] would have a non-existent object.

In that view, the very consequence of recognition being an error is the intended refutation. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (iṣṭāpatti), because if that were the case, since the cognition would be established by its very apprehension of non-difference, it would follow that pursuing the apprehension of "belonging to that same class" is redundant;
[the latter] is sought solely for the purpose of establishing the validity of the cognition.
It should be understood that "by following that" means that even by following that [view], there is no remedy for the other [fault].

He dispels the misconception that the phrase "in the position of momentary consciousness" (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna-pakṣe*) has the meaning of "in the position of momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatva-pakṣe*) by stating "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*). This is because two refutations will be stated later in the root text.
Having formulated two possible objections, he connects them with the words "of the mere self" (*ātmamātrasya*).

"The state of having some indeterminate object" (*yatkiṃcidviṣayakatva*) means "the state of having one specific, fixed object. This is because, if taken literally, since it would have to be established according to experience that [cognition] has only a fixed "some-thing" as its object, an inconsistency would arise.

"Having that as its object" (*tadviṣayakatva*). Thus, because it follows from experience, there is no room for a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the postulation; this is the intended meaning. [Rāmarudrī:
"Of having an object" (*saviṣayakatvasya*). For it is not the case that [the cognition] has a jar as its object, but rather...
The underlying intention of the root text is that there is indeed the experience: "I am the possessor of the cognition whose object is the jar. Regarding the phrase "otherwise":

[one might object] that since the adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual souls (*jīva*) are infinite within the single Brahman, [the distinction between cognitions would be lost] due to the delimitation by their respective internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Regarding the doubt that the manifold experiences of distinct pleasure, pain, and so forth are not contradictory within a single [consciousness]—just as the experience of both sound and its absence is not contradictory in the same sky due to the delimitation by different ear-cavities—it is said in the root text, "otherwise" (*anyathā*). To explain its meaning, he says: "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*). The term "saṃsārī" means one who is bound.

The commentary: "Liberated" means one for whom saṃsāra has ceased. He states the reason why [the other view] would be untenable: "of Caitra and Maitra, the two selves. This means "of the two selves, the bound and the liberated.
"Of the two natures of the Lord" means "of the two natures of the single Lord. This...

And this has been stated as the reason for their unity. Now, regarding the two [consciousnesses] delimited by their respective internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which are both of the nature of the one Lord—this too has been stated as the reason for their unity. Furthermore, even though the consciousness delimited by each respective internal organ is one, that internal organ...

If it is argued that there is no inconsistency in the distinction between the bound and the liberated—since the convention of "liberation" applies to the consciousness delimited by that internal organ which has been destroyed, while the convention of being "bound" applies to the consciousness delimited by that internal organ which has not been destroyed—then [we reply]: [This is not so. For, if the internal organ were destroyed, its substrate (the Self) would also be destroyed, because the internal organ is non-different from its substrate; and thus, since the substrate would be absent, liberation would be impossible. Furthermore, if the internal organ were not destroyed, bondage would persist, because the internal organ is the cause of bondage. Moreover, since the internal organ is non-different from its substrate, the destruction of the internal organ would entail the destruction of the substrate as well. Consequently, the very possibility of liberation would be undermined. Therefore, this position is untenable.

Even so, the point is that since the failure of the exertion undertaken for the sake of liberation remains unavoidable, even upon the destruction of this internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), suffering would necessarily arise in the Self as delimited by another internal organ; thus, the fruit of one's activity—the state of being free from suffering—would be impossible. If...
If it is asserted that pleasure, pain, and so forth belong only to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and never to consciousness (*caitanya*),

then effort for the sake of liberation would be entirely futile, because [consciousness] is eternally liberated by its very nature. And if it is further asserted that such effort is for the purpose of removing delusion, even then, [the problem remains] when [consciousness] is delimited by another internal organ.

The sense is that, since error must necessarily reside in oneself, effort would result in futility; therefore, such [effort] is necessary. "Difference" (bheda) means duality (dvitva). This is because, according to the literal reading, one would have to accept the destruction of difference.

Furthermore, it should be noted that since the root cause of the production of difference has not been stated, it would follow that the establishment of difference is inconsistent. Nor should it be argued that, due to the absence of an obstacle upon the destruction of difference, identity (*tādātmya*) might also arise.
The point is that if identity were to arise merely through the cultivation of non-difference, then it would follow that even a jar and a cloth would possess such a status [of identity].
— Rāmarudrī.
The phrase "the state of being empty of properties distinct from itself" is to be construed with what follows as "is not untenable.

Regarding the term "in the second [case]": the meaning is that in the second position, the nature of knowledge does not belong to the universal self (*ātmasāmānya*), but rather to the supreme self (*paramātman*) alone. Regarding the term "possessive suffix": this refers to suffixes such as *matup* (and others), which signify "that which has this" (*tad asyāsti*).

The meaning is that the suffix *aT* is prescribed by the rule *arśa-ādibhyo’j*. The reason given for the impossibility of its being neuter is that, according to the lexicon (*kośa*) which states "syād ānandathur ānandaḥ," it is determined to be invariably masculine; nor is it a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

It should be stated that this is the neuter gender. It should be noted that the acceptance of Vedic usage is justified only when there is no other alternative. [The word] "necessary" is used because the sense is that non-difference can only be construed with something other than pleasure (sukha) in relation to Brahman. Now, an objection:
Since it must be stated that Brahman is connected [to the negative particle] precisely as the substratum for the distinction of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), he says "otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "as the meaning of a noun": the point is that if one accepts the cognition of a connection between the meanings of two nouns as being distinct, then even in the case of "the king's man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*), there would result the undesirable cognition "the man belongs to the king" (*rājakīyaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is a particle" (*nipātatvāt*):

the rule that there is a relation of identity (*abheda*) only between the meaning of a nominal stem and the meaning of a nominal stem—excluding particles—is established. Otherwise, how could [the relation] in cases such as "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) be explained, where the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) [of the jar] is with respect to the absence (*abhāva*), which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)?
The sense is that there is an acceptance of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the jar and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having the same grammatical number" (*samānavacana*):

the sense is that the rule of having the same grammatical number applies only in cases where there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*). Regarding the phrase "due to contradiction with the suffix": this refers to the use of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as "one for whom happiness does not exist" (*na vidyate sukhaṃ yasya*).
The point is that [the view] contradicts the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of the *matvartha* suffix *ac* in the word "ānanda.

In reality, it is not well-known for the word "context" (*prakaraṇa*) to have the meaning of a suffix; therefore, "context" here refers precisely to the state of being recited as a series of words formed by a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*).

The meaning is "because of its contradiction with that. Since we observe *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compounds throughout passages such as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short... and so forth, it is more appropriate to interpret the meaning here as a contradiction of the context, given that the single word *asukham* is formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound in close proximity to those [compounds].

It occurs to me. He states the meaning of the phrase "by that which is rooted in the source" as follows: "as previously stated," etc. Furthermore, even in the Sāṃkhya system, it is not merely a person (puruṣa), but rather, because consciousness (caitanya) is admitted by the term "conscious" (cetana), and because consciousness is of the nature of knowledge, [it belongs] to the Self (ātman).

It should not be said that this is irrelevant because it is impossible to refute the Sāṃkhya doctrine by means of proving [the self] as possessing knowledge; for in their system, they admit that the conscious principle (*cetana*) is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), otherwise,
if one were to admit a knowledge distinct from the conscious principle, it would not be included within the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

The sense is that this would result in an excess of categories (*tattva*), because of their established doctrine: "Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification (*avikṛti*); the seven beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) are both nature and modification (*prakṛtivikṛti*); the sixteen are modifications (*vikāra*); and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor modification."

He states another meaning of the word "etena" (by this) as "vakṣyamāṇa" (to be described). "Mūla" means "the cause of all. "Prakṛtitva" means "causality. [Objection: But why is it that being a possessor of a favorable effort (*anukūlakṛtimattva*) alone constitutes agency (*kartṛtva*)?

Since this is not accepted, he says: "anukūla" (conducive). Regarding the phrase "mābhavatviti" (let it not be): the sense is that if the Puruṣa were the cause of things such as a jar, then even the effect, such as the jar, would not undergo destruction; for there is no difference between cause and effect, and because the Puruṣa is immutable, a modification in the form of destruction is impossible for him.

"By means of the channel of the sense organs" (indriyapraṇālikayā) means "through the door of the sense organs. According to this principle, when the intellect (buddhi), having gone outward through the path of the sense organs, reaches the location of an object such as a jar, a transformation of the intellect arises in the form of that [object]; that very [transformation] is the cognition of the jar and so forth, which takes the form of a mental modification (vṛtti). Thus [is the function] of the sense organs.

The state of being a door (*dvāratā*) is to be understood as follows: the relation between the cognition and the jar is precisely their having the same form (*svākārakatva*). "Having the same form" means having the form of the object, such as the jar.
"Transformative nature" (*pariṇāmitva*) means causality. "Not having an ungrasped non-relation" means not having an ungrasped difference.

It should be understood that the non-apprehension of difference arises solely from defects in the form of proximity to the intellect (*buddhi*). The concealment of essential nature (*svarūpa-tirodhāna*) is the non-manifestation of an intrinsic being devoid of all relations; it is the delimitation by the object (*viṣayāvaccheda*).

The manifestation of a connection with an object; the meaning of "in isolation" (kaivalyena) is likewise "without the manifestation of a connection with an object. "Of the intellect alone" (buddher eva): the sense is that suffering and its destruction arise only within the intellect. Direct connection.

The meaning is that it consists of a relation of essential nature (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Having raised the objection that the intellect’s being related to the *puruṣa* would be untenable without such a relation to the *puruṣa*, he says "of the intellect" (*buddhi-*), etc.
Thus, the point is that the relation there is simply the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*). Independently...

"Beyond the non-apprehension of difference" (*bhedāgrahātirekeṇa*) is stated for the purpose of presenting the evidence for postulating a direct relation (*sākṣātsambandha*). "Of that direct relation" (*tasya sākṣātsambandhasya*). "If it were based on the nature of the Person" (*puruṣasvabhāvaniṣbandhatve*) means if it were necessitated by the essential form of the Person (*puruṣasvarūpaprayuktatve*). [This refers to] a relation whose own essence is its very form (*svātmakasvarūpasambandhasya*).

The sense is that [the manifestation] is dependent upon its own inherent nature (*svasvabhāva*). Anticipating the complexity of postulating the aforementioned intention, he introduces this very passage by another method, beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the adjunct of the person (*puruṣa*) and the adjunct of the object": the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and the meaning of that [case ending] is as follows:

The word *adhyavasāya* (determination) has a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with the object of the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) into the form of knowledge. The genitive case in the phrase "of the jar and so forth to be made" (*kartavyaghaṭādeḥ*) also connects to that very same [object]. Regarding the phrase "the factor of activity" (*vyāpārāṃśa*):
it refers to that which possesses a part (*aṃśa*), namely a relation (*saṃbandha*), which is designated as "activity" (*vyāpāra*) or "that which is to be done" (*kartavya*).

The meaning is "so it is. And thus, in the verbal expression of the cognition "this must be done by me," the connection with the person is denoted by the word "by me" (namā), the connection with the object by the word "this" (idam), and the connection with the activity by the word "must be done" (kartavyam); therefore, [the cognition] possesses these three relations.

The meaning is that "apprehension" (upalabdhi) refers to that unreal relation— which is perceived as "this knowledge [of the object] is together with the knowledge of the person superimposed upon the Buddha"—
and this is to be understood by supplying the word "pratīyamānaḥ" (being perceived) through the process of mental synthesis (yojanā).
